1 Welcome to the monthly newsletter from the Ada County Board of Commissioners. We are happy to share information on significant news and events in Ada County. Ryan Davidson - Commissioner Tom Dayley - Commissioner Rod Beck - Chairman NEWS FROM THE BOARD NEWS FROM THE BOARD MONTHS BEFORE OPENING, ADA COUNTY’S PARK AT EXPO IDAHO WINS INTERNATIONAL AWARD We still have several months to go before Ada County’s Park at Expo Idaho opens and already the accolades for this unique regional destination park underscore how remarkable this once in a generation 50-acre park will be. The World Landscape Architecture Awards (WLA) are a prestigious global award program recognizing the best of the best in landscape architecture. More than 275 entries worldwide were submitted and Ada County’s Park at Expo Idaho received the top Award of Excellence in the Concept/Public Space Design category. July 2026 A monthly newsletter from the Ada County Board of Commissioners

# Page 4^page=4
4 ADA COUNTY CELEBRATES 100TH DRUG COURT GRADUATION CEREMONY Exceedingly successful program changes lives and promotes stability “How do we know Ada County’s Drug Court Program works? Because we can count.” That’s the quote the Honorable District Judge James Cawthon shared with individuals and families at the July 14, 2026 Drug Court graduation ceremony at the Ada County Courthouse in Boise. The Honorable retired District Judge Michael Reardon first coined that phrase years ago and it resonates now more than ever. The inspiring and joyous ceremony marked the 158th commencing class of the county’s drug court program. Eleven proud and smiling graduates were on hand with friends and family to mark their new beginnings. Bryce Nearman "Drug Court gave me the opportunity to make mistakes, learn from them, and keep moving forward instead of being defined by them. The accountability it provided helped me stay sober while teaching me self-discipline for the first time in my adult life. That discipline didn't just help me recover—it changed the direction of my life." Jonathan Wolfe "Drug Court has given me the opportunity to make change in every aspect of my life. If it wasn’t for Drug Court, I would’ve missed out on the first two years of my daughter’s life. But instead, I have been able to buy a house and support my family. I have also been able to grow with time management skills and develop personal goals. Drug Court has been the forefront of my recovery and my sobriety in the community”

# Page 5^page=5
5 Drug Court graduations are deeply meaningful. The graduates have reached one of the most important milestones in their lives. The stories they share are remarkable testaments to the resilience of the human spirit. Stories often center on hitting rock bottom and being filled with guilt and remorse, and then just a few years later being able to stand before their fellow graduates, their loved ones and the world with gratitude and purpose. Ada County’s Drug Court program is one of five treatment court programs - three Drug Courts, one Veterans Treatment Court and one Mental Health Court. The statistics for Drug Court are noteworthy. • The typical length of time it takes to complete the program is 22+ months. • 96% of graduates are employed at graduation. • The positive economic impact on our community tops $35 million. • 19% of graduates returned to school to earn their GEDs or to attend college and most importantly, 162 drug-free babies are born to women in Drug Court.

# Page 6^page=6
6 “We have countless programs within Ada County government that make our communities stronger and safer,” said Ada County Commissioner Ryan Davidson. “Drug Court stands apart as a shining example of how government can in many ways change the course of someone’s life forever in a positive way. Everyone at some point in their life needs an outstretched hand. We are grateful to everyone who extends those hands.” “Ada County’s Drug Court program not only changes the lives of the graduates,” said Ada County Commission Chairman Rod Beck, “It changes entire families. Bonds are reestablished and families are made whole again. But most importantly, these individuals are now able to fully realize the talent and goodness they have within themselves.” “Every person has within themselves a light that cannot be extinguished,” said Ada County Commissioner Tom Dayley. “To know that so many bright and talented individuals can now shine their light without the weight of addiction and chaos is truly remarkable and inspiring. The board is deeply grateful for the talented counselors, judges, UA techs, Parole Officers, mentors and support staff who have a pivotal role in keeping those lights shining.”

# Page 8^page=8
8 THE STORY OF THE ADA COUNTY SEAL 2026 is a year of major historic milestones both nationally and here at home. Even the Ada County Seal has reached an important benchmark. When you see the Ada County seal on documents, outside buildings and on emails, you may wonder about its origins. We have answers. Ada County’s Human Resources Department Director Bethany Calley presented a special plaque to the Ada County Commissioners to mark the 40th anniversary of the county’s seal last month. Adopted on June 5, 1986, to represent the heritage, values, and identity of the people of Ada County, the seal was designed by Captain Gil Wright of the Ada County Sheriff’s Office. It portrays an early-morning easterly view of the majestic Rocky Mountain panorama and the national forests surrounding the county’s fertile Snake River agricultural plain. The eagle in flight represents the county’s natural wildlife and the World Center for Birds of Prey. The three stars signify the three branches of county government and the three elective districts of Ada County. Ada County is truly a special place with a special story! Pictured L-R: Ada County Commissioner Tom Dayley, Ada County Commissioner Ryan Davidson, Ada County Commission Board Chair Rod Beck, Ada County Human Resources Director Bethany Calley, and Ada County Sheriff Matt Clifford

9 52ND STREET BRIDGE A VERY WELCOME ADDITION IS IN THE WORKS If you use and love the Boise River Greenbelt behind Ada County’s Park at Expo Idaho and you enjoy riding through Garden City your ride or walk will soon be even more enjoyable. The Foundation for Ada/Canyon Trail Systems (FACTS) presented the Ada County Board of Commissioners with a check for more than $17,000 during the Board’s Open Business Meeting (OBM) Tuesday July 28, 2026. Garden City applied for the federal grant and later turned the project over to Ada County. The federal funds require a 7.34% local match. This long-planned connection will: • Remove a half-mile on-street detour • Improve safety for pedestrians and cyclists • Expand access across the Treasure Valley Greenbelt system Pictured L-R: Ada County Commissioner Ryan Davidson, Bob Hay, FACTS; Jim Szatkowski, President, Boise Exchange Club; Judy Peavey-Derr, Founder and Donation Director, FACTS; Bill Mullane, Vice President, FACTS; Ada County Commissioner Tom Dayley; Ada County Commission Chairman Rod Beck.

# Page 10^page=10
10 LEARN MORE ABOUT ACHD VEHICLE REGISTRATION FEES This November, Ada County voters will see a ballot measure asking whether to continue the Ada County Highway District (ACHD)’s local Vehicle Registration Fee (VRF). When you register an eligible vehicle in Ada County, a portion of those fees goes to ACHD (which is a separate entity from Ada County Government). The money collected from VRF helps fund roadway improvements that support road and bridge repair, congestion relief, and safe routes to school for Ada County residents. ACHD currently collects around $14 million annually in VRF. ACHD first began collecting VRF in 1990, after a ballot measure was approved by Ada County voters. The program was renewed by another ballot measure in 2008. The current fees are scheduled to sunset in 2028. This upcoming ballot measure, if approved by Ada County voters, would extend the current fees to 2046. ACHD is electing not to propose an increase in the current fees, which have been in place since 2008. For most passenger vehicles, the VRF that Ada County collects works out to between $0.46 and $0.77 per week. Current fee rates are: For each automobile, pickup truck, or motor vehicle with a maximum gross weight not exceeding 8,000 pounds, designed to carry passengers and not for hire: • Vehicles over seven years old: $24 • Vehicles between three and seven years old: $36 • Vehicles one to two years old: $40 • Motor vehicles primarily used for hire and each school bus: $16.00 • Motorcycles and terrain vehicles: $8.00 Residents can learn more about ACHD’s Vehicle Registration Fees, see project examples, get answers to frequently asked questions, and preview the official ballot language by visiting ACHD’s website: VEHICLE REGISTRATION FEES IN ADA COUNTY This article was submitted by the Ada County Highway District (ACHD). ACHD is a separate government agency responsible for local roadways in Ada County. IMPORTANT SURVEY - TAKES 5 MINUTES Photo courtesy Idaho News 6

11 FY27 ADA COUNTY BUDGET PRESENTATION Ada County Clerk Trent Tripple presented the FY27 Budget of $405 million to the Ada County Board of Commissioners on Tuesday July 21, 2026. The budget presentation included the opportunity for public input, although no members of the public were on hand to share any comments or concerns. Ada County offers a unique, award-winning tool that allows anyone to see exactly how their tax dollars are allocated. The Ada County Budget Explorer drills down into every department and office, showing you where and how your tax dollars are being used. Created by Clerk’s Office Performance Analyst Anthony Lock-Smith, this invaluable resource provides the kind of transparency in government our residents expect and depend on.

12 DAN HOGABOOM - 20 YEARS Congratulation to Dan Hogaboom for reaching a major milestone at Ada County. Dan joined the county in 2006 as a Support Operator and advanced through several technology support roles before becoming a Technology Asset Specialist in 2016. Known for his cheerful “good morning” and his signature response, “Happy to be here like always,” Dan brings a fun attitude to the workplace every day. Outside of work, he enjoys spending time with grandkids, gardening, and is always happy to share helpful tips and advice on what he’s currently growing. Here’s to twenty more years Dan! Pictured L-R: Luke ten Doeschate, IT Audio/Visual Technician; Stephen O’Meara, IT Director; Stacey Wall, Business Operations Manager IT; Dan Hogaboom, IT Technology Asset Specialist; Ada County Commissioner Tom Dayley, Ada County Commissioner Ryan Davidson. CENTRAL DISTRICT HEALTH WELCOMES NEW DIRECTOR The Ada County Commissioners are pleased to welcome Kristin Ryan as the new director of Central District Health (CDH). Ryan most recently worked at the City of Boise as Deputy Director of Public Works. Prior to that she was a Deputy Director for the Idaho Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ) for four and a half years. Before moving to Boise, Ryan held executive level positions in Alaska with the Department of Environmental Conservation and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency starting in 2002. CDH provides a vast array of essential services to our communities including administering the Women and Infant Children (WIC) program, conducting restaurant inspections, water/septic system inspections and communicable disease control. CDH is one of seven health districts in Idaho. The district includes Ada, Boise, Elmore and Valley Counties. Ryan succeeds Director Russ Duke who retired this year following 23 years of outstanding service.
